summary: The Service Registration Protocol uses ordinary DNS Update to enable DNS-based Service Discovery with only unicast packets. That avoids multicast, which scales poorly and works badly on networks such as Wi-Fi, and makes it practical to deploy service discovery at larger scale.

eli5.summary: Printers and speakers can announce themselves by signing up at a front desk rather than shouting across a noisy room. This is that front desk for DNS service discovery.

questions: what is the service registration protocol
how does srp register services in dns-sd
what is fcfs naming in srp
subtitle: How devices register their services with a DNS server over plain unicast, with no multicast needed.

tldr.problem: DNS-based Service Discovery over unicast works with many clients, but getting service data into DNS is hard: manual entry is costly, and plain DNS Update needs trust or shared secrets and many round trips.
tldr.mechanism: A device sends one DNS Update, signed with SIG(0) and carrying a lease, to an SRP registrar. The registrar applies fixed rules about which records are allowed and uses First Come, First Served naming to protect names.
tldr.outcome: Services can be registered and discovered with unicast only, but the protocol deliberately allows only a narrow set of records because no trust is established. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9665 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2025, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It relies on the lease option from RFC 9664, and the RFC itself says that future work might extend the allowed records or add an authorization model.

sections.title: Registering Services Without Multicast
sections.content:
DNS-based Service Discovery (RFC 6763) lets servers publish how to reach their services and lets clients find them. With Multicast DNS (RFC 6762) this happens on the local link. Using ordinary unicast DNS can be more efficient and versatile, but it is used much less because populating authoritative servers by hand is costly and error-prone, and plain DNS Update (RFC 2136) needs the server to trust updates or to share a secret or public key with the requester. It can also be chatty, with several round trips of conditional predicates.

The Service Registration Protocol (SRP) adds default rules so no predicates are needed: the SRP registrar applies built-in checks and the update either succeeds entirely or fails in a way the requester can understand. The RFC is candid that this is not a way to add arbitrary data to a zone. Because trust is not established, only a restricted set of records is accepted, and records such as SOA, MX and CNAME are forbidden. It is meant for solutions where multicast is inefficient or sleepy devices are common.
sections.eli5: Shouting across a crowded room works badly. SRP lets a device walk to the front desk and be written down in the list instead, but the desk only writes down a few safe kinds of information.

sections.title: Two Variants and Where to Register
sections.content:
SRP uses DNS Update with SIG(0) and comes in two variants. Full-featured hosts such as computers, laptops, printers, home routers and long-lived-battery phones either are configured with a registration domain or discover it with Domain Enumeration (RFC 6763, Section 11). They find the closest enclosing zone with SOA queries and then look up the SRV record _dnssd-srp._tcp.<zone> to find the registrar, or _dnssd-srp-tls._tcp.<zone> when they use TLS.

Constrained hosts, designed for constrained-node networks, register in the special-use name default.service.arpa., and the network supplies the list of registrars. The registrar may accept updates into a local zone or rewrite the names to ones with wider visibility. The split exists because discovering a registrar costs energy that low-power devices cannot spare, while networks that are not constrained can have more complicated topologies, which allows off-network spoofing. To guard against off-path spoofing, TCP is required on such networks.

IANA recorded service.arpa. as a special-use domain name, created a registry of its subdomains whose first entry is default.service.arpa., registered the service names dnssd-srp and dnssd-srp-tls (both TCP, no port number), and allocated the IPv6 anycast address 2001:1::3/128 as a default destination when no registrar is configured.
sections.eli5: Big devices look up the address of the front desk themselves. Tiny battery devices are simply told where it is when they join the network, which saves their batteries.

sections.title: What an SRP Update Contains
sections.content:
An SRP Update is a single DNS Update message with three kinds of instructions. A Service Discovery Instruction adds or deletes exactly one PTR record that maps a service type (or subtype) to a service instance name. A Service Description Instruction for each instance deletes all record sets at the instance name and then adds an SRV record, one or more TXT records, and optionally a KEY record. A Host Description Instruction does the same for the hostname, adding A or AAAA records and a KEY record.

There is always exactly one hostname per update, and every SRV target must be that hostname. The KEY record in a service description may be omitted, in which case the registrar behaves as if the host's KEY were given. An update must contain no prerequisites, and anything that cannot be identified as one of the three instruction types is not an SRP Update. Deletes must come before the adds they affect, which is the only ordering rule.

Requesters are told to combine changes into one update when possible, subject to size limits such as the roughly 500 bytes an IEEE 802.15.4 network handles well. If they cannot fit, they MUST send updates one at a time, not sending the next until the previous is acknowledged.
sections.eli5: The sign-up form has three parts: what kind of service you offer, the details of your particular service, and the name of the machine it runs on. You fill in all three on one page.

sections.title: First Come, First Served Naming
sections.content:
Shared secrets (TSIG, RFC 8945) do not suit automatic registration, so SRP uses First Come, First Served (FCFS) Naming. The requester signs the update with SIG(0) and includes its public key in KEY records. As long as the registrar remembers a name and its key, no other requester can add or update that name. A second requester that tries to claim it does not have the private key, so its claim is rejected, which forces it to pick a new name.

The RFC stresses that authenticate here only means telling that an update came from the same source as the original registration. No trust is established, which is why the allowed records are so restricted. Each name's protection lasts for the KEY lease, which can be longer than the lease on the other records. The registrar also checks existing KEY records against the ones in the update, and answers YXDomain if a name is already owned by a different key.
sections.eli5: Whoever writes a name on the list first owns it, and proves it with a secret signature only they can make. Someone else who tries the same name cannot copy the signature, so they must choose another name.

sections.title: What a Requester Does
sections.content:
The requester generates a public/private key pair that MUST be unique to the device and stored in stable storage (or preconfigured in read-only storage). A new key means a new name, since the old name belongs to the old key. The KEY record flags field MUST be all zeroes, and the same key must appear in every KEY record of the update.

If the registrar answers YXDomain, the requester MUST choose a new name or give up. A common approach is to append a number, for example trying host, host-1, host-2 and then a random number. If a name is refused with Refused, as when it is on a prohibited list, the requester should not just append a number and try again.

Lifetimes come from the Update Lease option (RFC 9664). The records other than KEY use the lease, typically two hours, so a disconnected device does not linger in user interfaces. The KEY lease SHOULD be much longer, typically 14 days, so another device cannot take the name the moment the device disappears.

To remove everything, the requester sends an update with a LEASE of zero containing exactly one Host Description Instruction with one Delete All RRsets From A Name instruction and no adds. The registrar then removes all service instances and PTR records pointing at that hostname. KEY-LEASE should also be zero if the removal is permanent, or kept unchanged to hold the name. To remove one service, the requester deletes its service instance name, but the hostname itself cannot be deleted that way. A requester MAY compress the target name in SRV records in an update, and registrars MUST support it.
sections.eli5: A device keeps its own secret stamp. If someone already took the name it wants, it tries a similar one, like adding a number. When it leaves for good, it hands in a request to remove all its entries.

sections.title: How the Registrar Validates an Update
sections.content:
The registrar first checks that the message is a valid DNS Update, with a single zone and every change inside that zone. An SRP Update MUST contain exactly one Host Description Instruction and an Update Lease option whose LEASE is no greater than its KEY-LEASE. A message that is not an SRP Update MAY be processed as a normal DNS Update, and otherwise MUST be rejected with Refused.

Next comes the name and signature check: if any existing KEY record does not match the one in the update, the registrar MUST reject with YXDomain. Otherwise it validates the SIG(0) signature against the host's KEY record, and a failure means Refused. After applying a valid update every updated service description MUST have a KEY identical to the host's. Registrars MUST implement ECDSAP256SHA256 for validation, and requesters MUST NOT assume algorithms numbered lower than 13 are available.

Subtypes are handled atomically: whatever subtypes appear in an update are the complete set, and any subtype missing from the update is removed. There is no way to delete a single subtype except by sending the others. Responses are NoError, ServFail, Refused or YXDomain, and the requester MUST NOT try to validate any records included in an error response.

Registrars MAY ignore addresses with too little scope, such as link-local ones, add a reverse-mapping PTR record, accept only pre-registered keys, or reject names from a dictionary of prohibited ones with Refused. All records in an RRset must carry the same TTL, and the registrar MUST reject updates where they differ.
sections.eli5: The desk follows a checklist. Is the form the right shape? Is the name already taken by someone with a different signature? Does the signature match? If anything is wrong, the form comes back with a reason.

sections.title: Leases, TTLs and Cleaning Up
sections.content:
Every SRP Update MUST include the Update Lease option, and registrars MUST reject updates that lack it. The response includes the granted lease, and the requester MUST use those times for renewing, whether shorter or longer. A default limit of two hours for the lease and 14 days for the KEY lease is thought to be a good choice, and registrars serving infrequently waking battery devices may need higher limits. Requesters SHOULD refresh well before a lease ends.

The lease belongs to the hostname. When it expires, the hostname and every service that references it MUST be removed together, along with the Service Discovery PTR records, though a KEY record may remain until the KEY lease ends. Registrars also track a lease per service instance, and remove an instance when its lease expires, so services a requester has forgotten about are not advertised forever.

Lease times and TTLs are unrelated. The TTL is a constant sent with each answer, while the lease is used only to decide when stale records are deleted. TTLs in an SRP Update are advisory, the registrar may override them, and they SHOULD NOT be longer than the lease time.
sections.eli5: Each entry on the list has a time limit and the device must come back to renew it. If the machine's entry expires, all the services listed under it go too.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
SRP has no authorization beyond first come, first served, so an outside attacker who knows the registrar's address could in principle get updates processed. Registrars SHOULD reject updates from outside their administrative domain. Over TCP, the three-way handshake blocks off-path forging, so registrars relying on it MUST NOT accept TCP Fast Open payloads. For UDP updates from constrained devices, spoofing must be stopped by source address filtering on routers.

Registering arbitrary names has risks too: requesters could register names like www or mail, or offensive names. The RFC recommends not offering SRP in organization-level zones, using a subdomain such as dnssd.example.com., and configuring a dictionary of prohibited names. Where an authoritative server also accepts other kinds of update, those must not be allowed to override records added by SRP. The protocol does not authenticate the registrar to the requester.

For privacy, since updates can be sent off-link, registrars MUST offer TLS and requesters SHOULD use DNS over TLS when available, though only as opportunistic privacy. Public keys can be used to track hosts, so a registrar MAY choose not to return KEY records in answers.
sections.eli5: The front desk trusts whoever shows up first, so it must be kept inside the building and should refuse silly or rude names. Writing on the list in a sealed envelope keeps nosy passers-by from reading it.
